chapters.chapter_title: The Rise of Nationalism in Europe

mind_map.root_topic: The Rise of Nationalism in Europe

branches.theme: The French Revolution and the Idea of the Nation

sub_branches.concept: Creation of Collective Identity (1789)
details: Transferred sovereignty from absolute monarchy to French citizens body.
Introduced la patrie (fatherland) and le citoyen (citizen) emphasizing equal rights under a constitution.
Adopted new French tricolour flag replacing the royal standard.
Established National Assembly elected by active citizens.
Centralised administrative system, uniform law code, standardized weights and measures.
Promoted French language over regional dialects to unify the nation.
evidence_or_examples: Commemorated martyrs, composed revolutionary hymns, and took collective oaths in the name of the nation.

sub_branches.concept: Napoleonic Code (Civil Code of 1804) & Territorial Expansion
details: Abolished all privileges based on birth, established equality before law, and secured property rights.
Exported administrative reforms to Dutch Republic, Switzerland, Italy, and Germany.
Abolished feudal system, freed peasants from serfdom and manorial dues.
Removed guild restrictions in towns, improved transport and communication systems.
Initial enthusiasm of conquered populations turned to hostility due to increased taxation, censorship, and forced conscription into French armies.
evidence_or_examples: French troops initially welcomed as 'harbingers of liberty' in Brussels, Mainz, Milan, and Warsaw.

branches.theme: The Making of Nationalism in Europe

sub_branches.concept: Mid-18th Century Social and Political Structure
details: Europe divided into autocratic monarchies, cantons, and duchies without national unity.
Habsburg Empire in Austria-Hungary was a multi-ethnic patchwork (Germans, Magyars, Italians, Poles, Slavs).
Dominant landed aristocracy was numerically small but socially and politically powerful, connected by French language and intermarriage.
Peasantry formed the vast majority of the population (serfs in East, small tenants in West).
evidence_or_examples: Aristocracy spoke French for diplomacy and high society across regional borders.

sub_branches.concept: Emergence of Liberal Nationalism & Zollverein
details: Middle class (merchants, industrialists, professionals) championed liberalism derived from Latin 'liber' (free).
Politically: Freedom of individual, equality before law, constitutional government, consent of governed, inviolability of private property.
Economically: Freedom of markets, abolition of state-imposed restrictions on movement of goods and capital.
39 states of German Confederation had 11 customs barriers and separate currencies/weights (e.g. ell measuring unit).
In 1834, Zollverein (Customs Union) formed under Prussian initiative: abolished tariff barriers and reduced currencies from 30+ to 2.
evidence_or_examples: A merchant travelling from Hamburg to Nuremberg in 1833 paid 5% duty at 11 customs checkpoints.

sub_branches.concept: A New Conservatism after 1815 & The Congress of Vienna
details: Following Napoleon's defeat at Waterloo (1815), European powers met at the Congress of Vienna hosted by Austrian Chancellor Duke Metternich.
Conservatives believed traditional institutions (monarchy, Church, social hierarchy, property, family) should be preserved.
Bourbon dynasty restored in France; series of buffer states created on French borders to prevent future expansion.
Kingdom of Netherlands created (including Belgium); Genoa added to Piedmont; Austria given control of Northern Italy; Prussia gained key western territories.
German Confederation of 39 states left untouched.
Imposed strict censorship laws to curb critical anti-autocratic ideas.
evidence_or_examples: Metternich organized European powers to suppress liberal movements post-1815.

sub_branches.concept: The Revolutionaries & Secret Societies
details: Repression forced liberal-nationalists underground into secret societies to train revolutionaries and spread ideas.
Giuseppe Mazzini (Italian revolutionary from Genoa, b. 1807): member of Carbonari, exiled in 1831 for Liguria uprising.
Founded Young Italy in Marseilles and Young Europe in Berne.
Envisioned unified democratic Italian republic; Metternich called him 'the most dangerous enemy of our social order'.
evidence_or_examples: Young Europe brought together like-minded young men from Poland, France, Italy, and German states.

branches.full_explanation: Revolutions led by educated liberal-nationalist middle-class across Europe.

sub_branches.concept: July Revolution (1830) & Belgian / Greek Independence
details: July 1830 Paris uprising overthrew Bourbon King Charles X, installing Louis-Philippe as constitutional monarch.
Sparked Belgian revolution breaking away from United Kingdom of Netherlands.
Greek War of Independence (1821-1832): Greek nationalists supported by West Europeans and Romantics against Ottoman Empire.
Treaty of Constantinople (1832) formally recognized Greece as an independent nation.
evidence_or_examples: English poet Lord Byron organized funds, fought in Greece, and died of fever in 1824.

sub_branches.concept: Romanticism, Language and National Feeling
details: Romanticism: Cultural movement emphasizing emotion, intuition, mystical feelings, folk culture (das volk, volksgeist).
Polish nationalism kept alive through music and language under Russian partition.
Karol Kurpinski celebrated national struggle through operas and folk dances (polonaise, mazurka).
Russian imposed Russian language in Polish schools; Polish clergy used Polish language for religious instruction as symbol of resistance, leading to exile to Siberia.
evidence_or_examples: Grimm Brothers collected German folktales to build a shared German linguistic and cultural identity.

sub_branches.concept: Hunger, Hardship, Popular Revolts & 1848 Revolutions
details: 1830s: Massive population growth, rural-to-urban migration, unemployment, competition from cheap British machine goods.
1845 Silesian Weavers Revolt: 12,000 weavers attacked contractor homes demanding higher wages; 11 shot.
1848 Paris Revolt: Food shortages and unemployment forced Louis-Philippe to flee; National Assembly proclaimed Republic with universal male franchise (above 21) and right to work.
1848 Frankfurt Parliament: 831 elected German middle-class representatives met at St. Paul Church to draft constitution for united Germany under constitutional monarchy.
King Friedrich Wilhelm IV of Prussia rejected crown offered by parliament; assembly disbanded by troops.
evidence_or_examples: Women participated actively in 1848 revolts but were denied voting rights, admitted only as observers to Frankfurt Parliament gallery.

branches.theme: The Unification of Germany and Italy & Strange Case of Britain

sub_branches.concept: Unification of Germany (1864–1871)
details: Prussia took leadership of German unification after 1848 liberal failure.
Chief Minister Otto von Bismarck engineered unification through policy of 'Blood and Iron' using Prussian army and bureaucracy.
Three wars over seven years against Denmark (1864), Austria (1866), and France (1870-71) ended in Prussian victory.
Kaiser William I proclaimed German Emperor in Hall of Mirrors at Versailles on January 18, 1871.
New state modernized currency, banking, legal, and judicial systems in Germany.
evidence_or_examples: Proclamation of German Empire held in unheated Hall of Mirrors at Palace of Versailles.

sub_branches.concept: Unification of Italy (1859–1870)
details: Italy split into 7 states; only Sardinia-Piedmont ruled by Italian dynasty (King Victor Emmanuel II).
Count Cavour (Prime Minister): Diplomatic alliance with France defeated Austria in 1859.
Giuseppe Garibaldi led 'Expedition of the Thousand' (Red Shirts) in 1860, driving Bourbon rulers out of Two Sicilies with peasant support.
Victor Emmanuel II proclaimed King of United Italy in 1861; Rome annexed in 1870.
evidence_or_examples: Illiterate southern Italian peasants thought 'La Talia' was Victor Emmanuel's wife!

sub_branches.concept: The Strange Case of Britain
details: Nation-state creation was a long, gradual parliamentary process, not sudden revolution.
British Isles inhabited by distinct ethnic groups: English, Welsh, Scot, Irish.
Act of Union (1707) between England and Scotland formed United Kingdom of Great Britain, repressing Scottish Gaelic language and Highland culture.
Ireland forcibly incorporated into UK in 1801 following failed 1798 revolt led by Wolfe Tone and United Irishmen.
British identity promoted via Union Jack flag, God Save Our Noble King anthem, and English language.
evidence_or_examples: Scottish Highlanders forbidden to speak Gaelic or wear traditional tartan dress.

branches.theme: Visualising the Nation & Nationalism and Imperialism

sub_branches.concept: Visual Allegories of the Nation
details: 18th and 19th century artists personified nations as female figures.
Marianne (France): Represented French Republic with red cap, tricolour, cockade; statues erected in public squares.
Germania (Germany): Wore crown of oak leaves signifying heroism; held sword, imperial eagle shield, and tricolour flag.
Allegorical attributes: Broken chains (freedom), breastplate with eagle (strength), olive branch (peace), black-red-gold tricolour (1848 flag).
evidence_or_examples: Marianne images printed on postage stamps and coins to mark national unity.

sub_branches.concept: Nationalism to Imperialism: The Balkan Crisis
details: Late 19th-century nationalism lost liberal democratic character, becoming aggressive expansionism.
Balkans: Multi-ethnic region (modern Romania, Bulgaria, Albania, Greece, Macedonia, Croatia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, Slovenia, Serbia, Montenegro) under Ottoman control.
Disintegration of Ottoman Empire and romantic nationalism made Balkans an explosive powder keg.
Balkan states fiercely jealous of each other, seeking territory at others' expense.
Major European powers (Russia, Germany, Austria-Hungary, Britain) rivalled for naval, military, and commercial dominance in Balkans, leading to WWI in 1914.
evidence_or_examples: Slavic ethnic groups fought for independence, turning the Balkans into the immediate spark for First World War.

branches.theme: The First World War, Khilafat and Non-Cooperation

sub_branches.concept: Impact of First World War & Idea of Satyagraha
details: WWI created economic crisis: custom duties raised, income tax introduced, war defense expenditure doubled prices (1913-1918).
Forced recruitment of soldiers in rural areas caused widespread resentment.
1918-19 and 1920-21 crop failures combined with influenza epidemic killed 12-13 million people (1921 Census).
Mahatma Gandhi returned from South Africa in Jan 1915; introduced Satyagraha—soul force emphasizing power of truth and non-violence without physical coercion.
Early local Satyagrahas: Champaran, Bihar (1917, indigo peasants); Kheda, Gujarat (1917, revenue relaxation during crop failure/plague); Ahmedabad (1918, mill workers).
evidence_or_examples: Gandhian satyagraha in Champaran forced colonial authorities to abolish oppressive tinkathia indigo system.

sub_branches.concept: Rowlatt Act (1919) & Jallianwala Bagh Massacre
details: Rowlatt Act passed hurriedly through Imperial Legislative Council despite unanimous Indian opposition.
Gave government power to repress political activities and detain political prisoners without trial for up to 2 years.
Gandhi launched nationwide Rowlatt Satyagraha with hartal on April 6, 1919.
On April 13, 1919 (Baisakhi Day), Brigadier-General Dyer enclosed peaceful crowd at Jallianwala Bagh, Amritsar, and opened fire, killing hundreds to 'create a moral effect'.
Violent strikes and clashes followed; Gandhi called off satyagraha seeing rising violence.
evidence_or_examples: Rabindranath Tagore surrendered his Knighthood in protest against Jallianwala Bagh atrocities.

sub_branches.concept: Khilafat Issue & Launch of Non-Cooperation Movement
details: Gandhi realized need to unite Hindus and Muslims for a broader movement.
Ottoman Turkey defeated in WWI; rumors spread of harsh peace treaty on Ottoman Emperor (Khalifa, spiritual head of Islamic world).
Khilafat Committee formed in Bombay (March 1919) by Ali brothers (Muhammad Ali and Shaukat Ali).
Nagpur Congress Session (Dec 1920) adopted Non-Cooperation program uniting Khilafat and Swaraj demands.
Hind Swaraj (1909): Gandhi declared British rule survived in India only because of Indian cooperation.
evidence_or_examples: Students surrendered government school seats, lawyers boycotted courts, and foreign cloth imports halved between 1921-22.

sub_branches.concept: Movement in Towns
details: Middle-class participation in cities: thousands of students left government schools/colleges; headmasters and teachers resigned; lawyers (Motilal Nehru, C.R. Das) gave up practices.
Council elections boycotted in most provinces except Madras (Justice Party of non-Brahmins felt entering councils gave power).
Economic impact: Foreign cloth boycotted, foreign cloth burned in bonfires, liquor shops picketed; import value dropped from Rs 102 crore to Rs 57 crore.
Movement slowed down because khadi cloth was expensive for poor, and alternative Indian educational institutions were slow to develop.
evidence_or_examples: Justice Party in Madras refused to boycott council elections to challenge Brahmin dominance.

sub_branches.concept: Rebellion in the Countryside (Awadh Peasants & Gudem Tribals)
details: Awadh: Peasants led by Baba Ramchandra (sanyasi who was earlier indentured labourer in Fiji) against talukdars/landlords demanding high rents and begar (unpaid forced labour).
Demands: Reduction of revenue, abolition of begar, social boycott of oppressive landlords (Nai-Dhobi bandhs).
Oudh Kisan Sabha set up in Oct 1920 by Jawaharlal Nehru and Baba Ramchandra; 300+ branches within a month.
Gudem Hills of Andhra Pradesh: Militant guerrilla movement led by Alluri Sitarama Raju against forest laws restricting entry, cattle grazing, and wood collection.
Raju claimed divine powers, urged wearing khadi and giving up drinking, but advocated violence to liberate India; executed in 1924.
evidence_or_examples: Peasants attacked landlord houses, looted grain hoards, and invoked Gandhiji's name to justify non-payment of rent.

sub_branches.concept: Swaraj in the Plantations
details: Assam tea plantation workers bound by Inland Emigration Act of 1859, which prohibited leaving tea gardens without permission (rarely granted).
For workers, Swaraj meant right to move freely and retaining link with native villages.
Thousands defied authorities, deserted plantations, and headed home believing 'Gandhi Raj' was coming.
Stranded by railway and steamer strikes, they were caught by police and brutally beaten.
evidence_or_examples: Plantation labourers marched away in thousands singing Gandhian slogans.

sub_branches.concept: Chauri Chaura Incident & Swaraj Party Formation
details: February 1922: Peaceful demonstration at Chauri Chaura (Gorakhpur, UP) turned violent; police station set on fire, killing 22 policemen.
Gandhi immediately called off Non-Cooperation Movement, feeling satyagrahis needed proper training before mass struggles.
C.R. Das and Motilal Nehru formed Swaraj Party within Congress to contest council elections and critique colonial policies from within.
Younger leaders like Jawaharlal Nehru and Subhas Chandra Bose pressed for radical mass agitation and full independence.
evidence_or_examples: Swarajists argued entering councils was vital to oppose colonial policies from inside government.

sub_branches.concept: Simon Commission & Lahore Congress (1929)
details: Tory government in Britain appointed Statutory Commission under Sir John Simon to review Indian constitutional system.
Commission had NO Indian members (all 7 British); arrived in 1928, met with nationwide protest slogan 'Go Back Simon'.
Lala Lajpat Rai assaulted by police during Simon Commission demonstration in Lahore, later succumbed to injuries.
Viceroy Lord Irwin offered vague 'dominion status' offer in Oct 1929 and Round Table Conference.
December 1929 Lahore Congress under Jawaharlal Nehru formalized demand for 'Purna Swaraj' (Complete Independence) and declared Jan 26, 1930 as Independence Day.
evidence_or_examples: Protesters waved black flags against Simon Commission across major cities.

sub_branches.concept: Salt March (Dandi March) & Civil Disobedience Launch
details: Gandhi sent 11 demands letter to Viceroy Irwin on Jan 31, 1930, including abolition of salt tax.
Salt tax selected because salt was consumed by rich and poor alike; tax and state monopoly revealed oppressive face of British rule.
Irwin refused negotiation; Gandhi started 240-mile Salt March from Sabarmati Ashram to Dandi with 78 trusted volunteers.
Walked 10 miles a day for 24 days; reached Dandi on April 6, 1930, manufactured salt by boiling seawater, breaking colonial law.
Signaled launch of Civil Disobedience Movement: people urged not only to withhold cooperation but to break colonial laws.
evidence_or_examples: Thousands across coastal India manufactured salt; foreign cloth picketed, peasants refused revenue/chowkidari taxes, forest people entered reserved forests.

sub_branches.concept: Repression, Gandhi-Irwin Pact & Movement Relaunch
details: Colonial government arrested Congress leaders (Abdul Ghaffar Khan in April 1930, Gandhi in May 1930).
Police attacked peaceful satyagrahis, beat women and children, arrested 100,000+ people.
Gandhi-Irwin Pact signed March 5, 1931: Gandhi called off Civil Disobedience and agreed to attend 2nd Round Table Conference in London; Irwin agreed to release non-violent political prisoners.
Conference failed; Gandhi returned empty-handed, found Ghaffar Khan and Nehru in jail, Congress declared illegal.
Gandhi relaunched movement in 1932; lost momentum by 1934.
evidence_or_examples: Sholapur industrial workers attacked police posts and municipal buildings after Gandhi's arrest.

sub_branches.concept: Social Groups Participation & Limits of Civil Disobedience
details: Rich Peasants (Patidars of Gujarat, Jats of UP): Active organizers protesting high revenue; disappointed when movement suspended without revenue cut.
Poor Peasants: Wanted unpaid rent to landlords cancelled; Congress hesitant to support 'no-rent' campaigns fearing alienation of rich landlords.

Business Classes (Purshottamdas Thakurdas, G.D. Birla): Formed Indian Industrial and Commercial Congress (1920) and FICCI (1927); supported movement to stop foreign imports but retreated after rising militant violence.
Industrial Workers: Limited participation except in Nagpur; struck at railway workshops and tin mines.
Women: Massive participation—marched, manufactured salt, picketed liquor/foreign cloth shops; seen by Gandhi as sacred duty of home.

Limits: Dalits (Depressed Classes) marginalized; Dr. B.R. Ambedkar clashed with Gandhi at 2nd Round Table Conference demanding separate electorates; settled via Poona Pact (Sept 1932) giving reserved seats in general electorate.
Muslim organizations alienated after Khilafat end and growing Hindu Mahasabha dominance; Mr. Jinnah demanded reserved seats in Central Assembly.
evidence_or_examples: Poona Pact guaranteed reserved seats for Depressed Classes while maintaining unified electorate.

sub_branches.concept: Cultural Personification, Songs & Folk Revival
details: Nationalism grew through experiences of struggle and cultural processes: allegory, folklore, songs, prints.
Bharat Mata image created by Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay in 1870s; wrote 'Vande Mataram' included in novel Anandamath.
Abanindranath Tagore painted Bharat Mata (1905) as an ascetic, calm, divine figure holding food, clothing, manuscript, and mala.

Folklore revival: Rabindranath Tagore in Bengal collected ballads, nursery rhymes, and myths; Natesa Sastri in Madras published massive 4-volume Tamil folktale collection 'The Folklore of Southern India'.
evidence_or_examples: Vande Mataram became the widely sung anthem during the Swadeshi movement in Bengal.

sub_branches.concept: National Flags & Reinterpretation of History
details: Swadeshi Movement Flag in Bengal (1906): Tricolour (red, green, yellow) with 8 lotuses (8 British provinces) and crescent moon (Hindus & Muslims).
Swaraj Flag designed by Gandhi (1921): Tricolour (red, green, white) with spinning wheel in center representing self-help.

Reinterpretation of History: British portrayed Indians as backward and incapable of self-governance; Indian historians wrote about glorious ancient achievements in architecture, science, math, law, and trade to instill national pride.
evidence_or_examples: Carrying Swaraj flag and holding it aloft during marches became a symbol of defiance.

chapters.chapter_title: The Making of a Global World

mind_map.root_topic: The Making of a Global World

sub_branches.concept: Silk Routes and Long-Distance Cultural Trade
details: Pre-modern links established by traders, travelers, priests, and pilgrims carrying goods, money, values, skills, ideas, diseases.
Silk Routes: Vibrant land and sea trade networks connecting Asia with Europe and Northern Africa.
Outbound trade: Chinese silk, pottery, Indian textiles and spices; Inbound trade: Precious metals (gold, silver) from Europe to Asia.
Cultural exchange: Christian missionaries, Muslim preachers, and Buddhism spread along Silk Routes.
evidence_or_examples: Chinese pottery travelled same routes as silk and textiles to Europe and West Asia.

sub_branches.concept: Food Travels: Spaghetti, Potato and Biological Conquest
details: Food items shared across continents: Noodles travelled from China to West to become spaghetti; Arab traders took pasta to 5th-century Sicily.
Christopher Columbus discovered America; common foods introduced to Europe/Asia: potatoes, soya, groundnuts, maize, tomatoes, chillies, sweet potatoes.
Potato transformed European diet: allowed poor to eat better and live longer; 1845-1849 Irish Potato Famine killed 1 million people when disease destroyed potato crop.
Biological Conquest of Americas: Spanish and Portuguese conquistadors used smallpox germs rather than military firepower.
Native Americans had no immunity to European diseases; smallpox wiped out entire communities, opening continent for colonization.
evidence_or_examples: Irish peasants relied so heavily on potatoes that 1,000,000 starved to death during 1845-1849 crop blight.

sub_branches.concept: Three Global Economic Flows & Corn Laws Abolition
details: World economy shaped by 3 flows: Trade in goods (cloth/wheat), Labour migration, Capital investment.
British Corn Laws: Restricted import of foreign corn to protect local landlords, driving up urban food prices.
Abolition of Corn Laws: Industrialists forced repeal; cheap imported grain flooded Britain, making domestic farming uncompetitive.
Impact: Lands left uncultivated, thousands of farm workers migrated to cities or emigrated to America and Australia.
Global agricultural boom: Railways connected farms to ports; ships transported grain across Atlantic.
evidence_or_examples: Emigration from Europe reached nearly 50 million people moving to America and Australia in 19th century.

sub_branches.concept: Technology, Refrigerated Ships & Colonial Expansion
details: Inventions (railways, steamships, telegraph) transformed global trade.
Refrigerated Ships (1870s): Allowed transport of perishable meat over long distances from America/Australia to Europe.
Impact: Meat prices dropped in Europe, enabling poor workers to add meat and butter to diet, reducing social unrest.
Colonial Expansion: 1885 Berlin Conference saw European powers draw straight lines on map to carve up Africa.

Rinderpest (Cattle Plague) introduced to Africa in late 1880s via infected cattle imported from Asia to feed Italian troops in Eritrea; killed 90% of African cattle, destroying local pastoral economy and forcing Africans into wage labor.
evidence_or_examples: Rinderpest wiped out 90% cattle, enabling European colonial powers to easily subjugate African populations.

sub_branches.concept: Indentured Labour Migration & Indian Trade in Empire
details: 19th-century indentured labor described as a 'new system of slavery': workers bound by contract to work 5 years on plantations.
Recruited from poor regions of UP, Bihar, Central India, Tamil Nadu to Trinidad, Guyana, Surinam, Fiji, Mauritius.
Agents gave false promises; workers created hybrid cultural expressions: Hosay carnival in Trinidad, Chutney music, Bob Marley's Rastafarianism.
Indian textiles hit by British tariffs; raw cotton exports to Britain rose (from 3% to 35% between 1812-1871) while manufactured cloth imports flooded India.
Multilateral Settlement System: Britain maintained trade surplus in India, using it to balance trade deficits with other European countries.
evidence_or_examples: V.S. Naipaul and Shivnarine Chanderpaul are descendants of Indian indentured laborers in Caribbean.

sub_branches.concept: WWI Economic Impact & Mass Production (Henry Ford)
details: WWI (1914-1918) was first industrial war: machine guns, tanks, aircraft, chemical weapons used on massive scale.
Killed 9 million, injured 20 million working-age men; transformed Britain from world creditor to debtor to US.
US Assembly Line Mass Production pioneered by Henry Ford at Detroit plant (Model T car).
Assembly line sped up output by forcing workers to repeat single task continuously; high wages ($5/day) offset worker stress and fueled consumer boom (cars, fridges, radios).
evidence_or_examples: Ford's Model T became world's first mass-produced car using conveyor belt system.

sub_branches.concept: The Great Depression (1929) & Impact on India
details: Causes: Agricultural overproduction led to falling prices; US withdrew foreign loans (cut by $1 billion); Wall Street Crash in Oct 1929.
Impact in US/Europe: 4,000+ banks collapsed, 110,000 companies failed, US unemployment rose to 25%, global trade collapsed by 50%.
Impact on India: Agricultural prices fell 50% (wheat prices dropped 50% between 1928-1934); peasants suffered while fixed-income urbanites gained.
Indian peasants sold gold and silver jewelry to survive; gold exports from India helped support British pound and global economic recovery.
evidence_or_examples: Jute growers of Bengal saw raw jute prices crash by over 60%, driving them into deep debt.

branches.theme: Rebuilding a World Economy: Post-War Era

sub_branches.concept: Bretton Woods Institutions (IMF & World Bank)
details: July 1944 United Nations Monetary and Financial Conference held at Bretton Woods, New Hampshire, USA.
Established International Monetary Fund (IMF) to deal with financial surpluses/deficits of member nations.
Established International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (World Bank) to finance post-war reconstruction.
Bretton Woods System based on fixed exchange rates: currencies pegged to US dollar, dollar convertible to gold at $35/ounce.
Western industrial powers (especially US with veto power) dominated decision-making.
evidence_or_examples: US held veto power over key IMF and World Bank decisions.

sub_branches.concept: Decolonisation, G-77 & Relocation of Production to Asia
details: Post-1945: Asian and African colonies achieved independence but faced poverty and lack of resources.
Developing nations did not benefit from Western economic growth; formed G-77 (Group of 77) demanding New International Economic Order (NIEO).
NIEO demands: Control over natural resources, fair prices for raw materials, better access for manufactured goods in developed markets.
Collapse of Bretton Woods (1970s): Shift to floating exchange rates; rise of private commercial bank lending to developing nations.
MNCs relocated production to low-wage Asian countries (China, Vietnam) to cut costs, driving modern economic globalization.
evidence_or_examples: China's low wages and economic reforms attracted massive foreign direct investment after 1978.

sub_branches.concept: Proto-Industrialisation Network
details: Proto-industrialisation: Large-scale international market production in rural countryside before factory system.
Town urban guilds held monopolies, restricted entry, and regulated prices/production.
Merchants moved to countryside, supplying advances to poor peasants and cottagers who lost common land access under enclosures.
Production process: Stapler bought wool -> Spinner spun yarn -> Weaver wove cloth -> Fuller gathered cloth -> Dyer colored cloth -> London finished cloth.
Each merchant controlled 20-25 workers at each stage of production.
evidence_or_examples: London was known as the 'finishing centre' where cloth was prepared before export.

sub_branches.concept: The Coming Up of the Factory
details: Earliest factories came up in England in 1730s; cotton led first phase of industrialization.
Richard Arkwright created the cotton mill, bringing machinery, workers, and raw material under one roof for centralized supervision.
Raw cotton imports skyrocketed from 2.5 million pounds in 1760 to 22 million pounds in 1787.
Iron and steel industry grew rapidly after 1840s with railway expansion, outpacing cotton exports by 1873.
evidence_or_examples: Centralized factory mills allowed strict quality control and division of labor impossible in scattered rural cottages.

sub_branches.concept: Preference for Hand Labour & Seasonal Demand
details: Victorian Britain had abundant cheap migrant labor; industrialists had no urge to invest in costly machines.
Seasonal industries: Gasworks (winter), Breweries (winter), Bookbinders/Printers (Christmas), Ship repair (winter) relied on seasonal hand workers.
Aristocrats and bourgeoisie preferred handmade goods: intricate designs, customized shapes symbolised refinement.
Machines made uniform, standardized goods for export to colonies.
evidence_or_examples: Mid-19th century Britain offered 500 varieties of hammers and 45 kinds of axes—producible only by skilled hand labor.

sub_branches.concept: Workers' Lives & Resistance to Spinning Jenny
details: Surplus labor created job insecurity; getting job depended on social networks and friendship links.
Job seekers spent nights under bridges or in casual night shelters/workhouses.
James Hargreaves invented Spinning Jenny (1764): single wheel turned multiple spindles, spinning several threads at once.
Women hand spinners attacked Spinning Jennies because machine threatened their traditional manual livelihoods.
Building activity (roads, railways, drainage, tunnels) after 1840s generated new urban employment opportunities.
evidence_or_examples: Violent attacks on Spinning Jennies continued for decades across English textile towns.

sub_branches.concept: Age of Indian Textiles & East India Company Rule
details: Indian fine cottons and silks dominated international trade before age of machine industries.
Surat (Gujarat) connected to Gulf/Red Sea ports; Hoogly (Bengal) connected to Southeast Asian ports.
European trading companies gained monopolies through royal charters, causing decline of old ports (Surat, Hoogly) and rise of colonial ports (Bombay, Calcutta).
East India Company eliminated Indian merchants/brokers, appointing paid agents called Gomasthas to supervise weavers, collect cloth, and inspect quality.
Company gave advance loans to weavers, binding them to sell exclusively to Company.
Clashes broke out: Gomasthas acted arrogantly, marched with sepoys, beat weavers for delivery delays; weavers deserted villages and migrated.
evidence_or_examples: Weavers in Carnatic and Bengal deserted villages and refused advances from Gomasthas.

sub_branches.concept: Manchester Comes to India
details: British cotton industrialists pressured government to levy import duties on Indian cloth and force East India Company to sell British goods in India.
By 1850, cotton imports from Manchester constituted 31% of Indian import value (over 50% by 1870s).
Indian handloom weavers faced dual crisis: domestic market flooded with cheap British machine cloth, and raw cotton prices skyrocketed due to US Civil War (1861) diverting American supply to Britain.
evidence_or_examples: Weavers could not get raw cotton at affordable prices during US Civil War.

branches.theme: Factories Come Up, Early Entrepreneurs & Market for Goods

sub_branches.concept: Pioneer Indian Industrialists & Capital Accumulation
details: Capital accumulated through opium trade with China and trade with Britain/Burma.
Dwarkanath Tagore (Bengal): Built 6 joint-stock companies in 1830s-40s.
Dinshaw Petit and Jamsetjee Nusserwanjee Tata (Bombay): Built vast textile and industrial empires.
Seth Hukumchand (Marwari businessman): Set up first Indian jute mill in Calcutta (1917); G.D. Birla did same.
Colonial restrictions: Indian merchants barred from trading with Europe in manufactured goods, restricted to raw material exports (cotton, opium, wheat, indigo).
evidence_or_examples: J.N. Tata set up the Tata Iron and Steel Company (TISCO) at Jamshedpur in 1907.

sub_branches.concept: Factory Workers, Jobbers & WWI Production Boom
details: Factories drew rural peasants who moved between village harvest and mill work.
Mill owners employed Jobbers (trusted old workers) to recruit new hands, demand gifts/money, and control workers' lives.
WWI Impact: British imports stopped as UK mills supplied war needs; Indian factories commissioned to supply army boots, jute bags, uniforms, tents.
Indian mill production boomed; after war, Manchester could never recapture its lost position in Indian market.
evidence_or_examples: Jobber became a figure of authority demanding bribes for securing mill jobs.

sub_branches.concept: Small-Scale Industries & Marketing Goods
details: Small-scale and handloom industries expanded in 20th century despite factory growth.
Weavers adopted Fly Shuttle: mechanical device operated by ropes/pulleys, speeding up weaving and enabling larger width cloth.
Advertisements created new consumer culture: British labels featured 'Made in Manchester' to guarantee quality.
Manufacturers printed images of Indian Gods (Krishna, Saraswati, Lakshmi) and historic royalty on calendars to make foreign goods familiar to illiterate masses.
evidence_or_examples: Images of deities on calendar prints gave divine approval to manufactured products.

chapters.chapter_title: Print Culture and the Modern World

mind_map.root_topic: Print Culture and the Modern World

sub_branches.concept: East Asian Woodblock Printing (China, Japan, Korea)
details: Hand printing originated in China, Japan, and Korea.
From AD 594: China printed books by rubbing paper against inked wooden blocks; paper was thin and porous, so books were folded and stitched as 'accordion books'.
Imperial state of China was major producer of print for civil service examination candidates.
17th century: Print expanded from scholar-officials to merchants and urban readers (fictional narratives, poetry, plays).
Japan: Buddhist missionaries from China introduced hand printing around AD 768-770.
Oldest Japanese book: Buddhist Diamond Sutra (AD 868) containing 6 sheets of text and woodcut illustrations.
Edo (modern Tokyo) visual print culture depicted urban life, artists like Kitagawa Utamaro developed Ukiyo-e ('pictures of the floating world').
evidence_or_examples: Utamaro's Ukiyo-e prints influenced European impressionist artists like Edgar Degas and Vincent van Gogh.

sub_branches.concept: Print Comes to Europe & Gutenberg's Movable Type Press
details: Chinese paper reached Europe via Silk Route in 11th century.
In 1295, Marco Polo returned to Italy from China bringing woodblock printing knowledge.
Luxury manuscripts copied by scribes on expensive vellum (animal skin parchment) for aristocrats; woodblocks used for cheap broadsheets and playing cards.
Johann Gutenberg (Mainz, Germany) invented movable metal type printing press in 1448.
Gutenberg drew on olive press technology and metal moulds used for trinket making.
First book printed: Gutenberg Bible (180 copies produced in 3 years).
Print Revolution: 1450-1500 saw printing presses set up across Europe; book production rose from 20 million to 200 million copies.
evidence_or_examples: Gutenberg Bible illuminations and borders were still hand-painted by artists to retain luxury appeal.

sub_branches.concept: New Reading Public, Religious Debates & Dissent
details: Print reduced cost/time of book production, transforming hearing public into a reading public.
Publishers printed popular ballads and folktales illustrated with woodcuts to reach illiterate audiences at taverns.
1517: Martin Luther wrote Ninety-Five Theses criticizing Roman Catholic Church practices (sale of indulgences), nailed text to Wittenberg church door.
Printed copies circulated rapidly; launched Protestant Reformation; Luther translated New Testament into German (5,000 copies sold in weeks).
Luther declared: 'Printing is the ultimate gift of God and the greatest one.'
Menocchio (Italian miller) reinterpreted Bible after reading cheap printed books; tried twice by Inquisition and executed for heresy.
Catholic Church compiled Index of Prohibited Books (1558) to control heretical publications.
evidence_or_examples: Catholic Church set up Index of Prohibited Books in 1558 to censor anti-clerical literature.

sub_branches.concept: The Reading Mania & Enlightenment / French Revolution Link
details: 17th-18th centuries: Literacy rates rose across Europe (60-80% in parts of Europe).
Cheap popular literature sold by peddlers: Penny chapbooks in England (sold by chapmen), Bibliothèque Bleue in France (low-priced blue-covered books).
Periodicals, newspapers, maps, scientific diagrams of Isaac Newton, and works of Voltaire and Rousseau printed widely.
Louis-Sébastien Mercier declared: 'The printing press is the most powerful engine of progress... tyrants of the world tremble!'
Print and French Revolution: 1. Popularized Enlightenment ideas of reason; 2. Created public culture of debate and dialogue; 3. Caricatures and literature mocked royal morality.
evidence_or_examples: Cartoons depicting French royalty enjoying luxury while commoners suffered circulated widely before 1789.

branches.theme: The Nineteenth Century Innovations & India and the World of Print

sub_branches.concept: 19th-Century Innovations & India's Manuscript Tradition
details: Press Innovations: Richard M. Hoe (New York) perfected power-driven cylindrical press (8,000 sheets/hour); offset press printed 6 colors at once; electrically operated presses introduced.
Publishing innovations: Cheap series, paperbacks, dust jackets, serialised novels in periodicals.
India's Manuscript Tradition: Rich handwritten manuscripts in Sanskrit, Arabic, Persian, and vernaculars copied on palm leaves or handmade paper.
Manuscripts were fragile, expensive, difficult to read (written in different scripts), and not used in day-to-day schooling.
evidence_or_examples: Students in Bengal village schools learned to write from memory without reading printed textbooks.

sub_branches.concept: Print Comes to India & Religious / Social Reform Debates
details: Portuguese Jesuits brought first printing press to Goa in 1557; printed Tamil/Konkani tracts.

1780: James Augustus Hickey published Bengal Gazette ('a weekly political and commercial paper open to all, influenced by none'); Governor-General Warren Hastings prosecuted Hickey for criticizing royal officers.
Religious Reform Debates: Rammohun Roy published Sambad Kaumudi (1821) against Sati, idol worship, and caste abuses.
Hindu orthodox countered with Samachar Chandrika.
Muslim Ulema used Deoband Seminary (founded 1867) lithographic presses to issue fatwas instructing Muslims on code of conduct.
Naval Kishore Press (Lucknow) and Shri Venkateshwar Press (Bombay) published mass vernacular religious texts (Ramcharitmanas).
evidence_or_examples: Bengal Gazette editor James Hickey was persecuted by Warren Hastings for publishing gossip about colonial officials.

branches.theme: New Forms of Publication, Women, Caste & Censorship

sub_branches.concept: New Visual Forms, Women Readers & Autobiographies
details: Visual Culture: Raja Ravi Varma produced mass printed images of deities and myths; lithographic presses made visual art cheap.
Women and Print: Conservative Hindus believed educated women would be widowed; Muslims feared educated women would be corrupted by romances.
Rashsundari Debi (Bengal): Secretly learned to read in kitchen; wrote autobiography Amar Jiban (1876), first full-length autobiography in Bengali.
Kailashbashini Debi wrote books detailing harsh treatment of women in households.
Tarabai Shinde and Pandita Ramabai (Maharashtra) wrote passionate critiques of upper-caste Hindu patriarchal oppressions.
evidence_or_examples: Rashsundari Debi hid single manuscript pages behind kitchen stove to teach herself Bengali literacy.

sub_branches.concept: Print and the Poor / Anti-Caste Literature
details: Cheap small books sold at crossroads enabled poor workers to read.
Public libraries established by wealthy patrons or local associations in towns.
Jyotiba Phule wrote Gulamgiri (1873) dedicating it to Americans who fought to abolish slavery, attacking caste system injustices.
Dr. B.R. Ambedkar (Maharashtra) and E.V. Ramaswamy Naicker (Periyar in Madras) wrote powerful anti-caste publications.
Kanpur millworker Kashibaba wrote Chhote Aur Bade Ka Sawal (1938); Sudarshan Chakr wrote Sacchi Kavitayan under pen name.
evidence_or_examples: Millworkers in Kanpur set up their own libraries to educate themselves and discuss caste inequalities.

sub_branches.concept: Print and Censorship: Vernacular Press Act (1878)
details: Before 1798: East India Company concerned only about European critics in India attacking Company governance.
1835: Thomas Macaulay revised press laws to restore freedom to Indian press.
Post-1857 Revolt: Colonial government demanded strict control over nationalist Indian newspapers.
Vernacular Press Act (1878) passed by Lord Lytton (modeled on Irish Press Laws): gave government power to censor reports and editorials in vernacular papers.
If newspaper published seditious report, received warning; if ignored, press was seized and machinery confiscated.
Nationalist response: Nationalist papers grew rapidly; Balgangadhar Tilak wrote passionately in Kesari, leading to his imprisonment in 1908 and widespread protests.
evidence_or_examples: Amrita Bazar Patrika turned into an English newspaper overnight to escape the Vernacular Press Act!
